title: [Cache] EnableHeuristicFreshness is a no-op by default and applies a fixed lifetime to any 2xx regardless of status or Last-Modified
body:
## Summary
Heuristic freshness only takes effect when DoNotCacheWithoutFreshness is also false, so enabling EnableHeuristicFreshness alone does not cache Last-Modified-only responses. When active it applies one fixed lifetime to every 2xx response instead of restricting to heuristically cacheable status codes and deriving the lifetime from Last-Modified. A 202 job-status poll can be served from cache for a minute.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheInterceptor.cs:643`

## Problem
In PrepareEntryForStorage the DoNotCacheWithoutFreshness test returns before the heuristic assignment (CacheInterceptor.cs:638-644), so `EnableHeuristicFreshness = true` alone changes nothing except for no-cache entries, which are never served fresh anyway; Documentation~/Modules/Interceptors.md:148 describes the flag as a self-sufficient opt-in. When both flags are set, every status that ShouldConsiderForStorage admits (all 2xx except 206, :807-809) gets `now + HeuristicFreshnessLifetime`, including 201/202/205 that RFC 9111 section 4.2.2 does not make heuristically cacheable, and the lifetime ignores Last-Modified.

**Failure scenario.** `new CachePolicy { EnableHeuristicFreshness = true }`: a response with only Last-Modified is still not cached. With DoNotCacheWithoutFreshness=false as well, `202 Accepted` to a GET job-status poll without cache headers is served from cache for a minute.

## Spec reference
RFC 9111 4.2.2

## Suggested fix
Let EnableHeuristicFreshness imply storing responses that have Last-Modified, restrict heuristics to the heuristically cacheable status codes (IsRfc9111CacheableByDefault plus 200/203/204), and derive the lifetime from (Date - Last-Modified) / 10 capped by HeuristicFreshnessLifetime.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] EnableHeuristicFreshness alone causes responses with Last-Modified to be stored
- [ ] Heuristics apply only to heuristically cacheable status codes (RFC 9111 section 4.2.2) and the lifetime is derived from (Date - Last-Modified) / 10, capped by HeuristicFreshnessLifetime

title: [Cache] CacheInterceptor merges a 304 into the stored entry without checking that its ETag matches the stored validator
body:
## Summary
On a 304 the interceptor updates the stored response without comparing the 304's ETag with the stored one. A non-conforming origin or intermediary returning a different ETag makes the entry pair the old body with the new validator, so later revalidations succeed and the stale body is kept as validated indefinitely.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheInterceptor.cs:683`

## Problem
MergeNotModifiedEntry copies every header of the 304 except the framing ones into the stored headers (CacheInterceptor.cs:683-703) and then takes ETag and Last-Modified from the merged set (:724-725) while keeping `existing.Body` (:751). Nothing compares the 304's ETag with `existing.ETag`. RFC 9111 section 4.3.4 selects the stored response to update by the 304's strong validator and says that if none matches the cache must not update a stored response.

**Failure scenario.** A non-conforming origin or intermediary answers `If-None-Match: "v1"` with 304 and `ETag: "v2"`. The entry now pairs the v1 body with validator v2; all later revalidations send `If-None-Match: "v2"`, the origin correctly answers 304, and the client keeps serving the v1 body as validated for as long as v2 is current.

## Spec reference
RFC 9111 4.3.4

## Suggested fix
When the 304 carries an ETag that does not match the stored one (weak comparison is enough for GET), do not merge: drop the entry and refetch unconditionally.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A 304 whose ETag does not match the stored ETag (weak comparison) is not merged; the entry is dropped and the resource is refetched unconditionally
- [ ] A 304 with a matching or absent ETag still merges as before
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [Cache] CacheInterceptor builds cache entries in two diverged copies of the storability logic (store and 304 merge)
body:
## Summary
Entry construction at store time and in MergeNotModifiedEntry are separate copies of the same policy logic that have diverged. A 304 carrying no-store, or private with AllowPrivateResponses=false, produces a stored and served entry while the same fields on a 200 would prevent storage.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheInterceptor.cs:707`

## Problem
PrepareEntryForStorage (CacheInterceptor.cs:573-668) and MergeNotModifiedEntry (670-764) both resolve Vary, the sensitive-Vary policy, Date/response delay, expiry, validators, mustRevalidate, the freshness/heuristic block and the key/signature (609-649 vs 707-745). Only the first checks no-store, private with AllowPrivateResponses=false and the Authorization rule (596-607); the merge handles Set-Cookie with separate code (694-697). StorePreparedEntryAsync (968-987, swallows faults) and StorePreparedEntryCoreAsync (1039-1048, propagates) are a second diverged pair.

**Failure scenario.** A 304 carries 'Cache-Control: no-store, max-age=60' (the origin changed its policy), or 'private' with AllowPrivateResponses=false: the merged entry is stored and served as fresh for 60 s, while the same header fields on a 200 would have prevented storage.

## Spec reference
RFC 9111 section 3, 4.3.4

## Suggested fix
Extract one 'evaluate storability and build entry' function taking (request headers, status, effective response headers, body, times) and call it from both paths; keep a single store routine with an explicit fault policy.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One shared function evaluates storability and builds the entry from (request headers, status, effective response headers, body, times) and is called from both the store and the 304 merge paths
- [ ] The same header fields give the same storage decision on a 200 and on a 304 merge

title: [Cache] The 304 merge path skips the no-store and private storability checks that the 200 path applies
body:
## Summary
When revalidation returns 304 with Cache-Control: no-store, or private with AllowPrivateResponses=false, or the request had no-store, the entry is rewritten and still served as a HIT. The 200 path would have refused or evicted it. A resource that became sensitive stays cached for the new max-age.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheInterceptor.cs:722`

## Problem
PrepareEntryForStorage rejects on response/request no-store (CacheInterceptor.cs:603-604), on private when the policy forbids it (:606-607) and on the Authorization rule (:596-601). MergeNotModifiedEntry parses the merged Cache-Control (:722) but reads only max-age, no-cache, must-revalidate and stale-while-revalidate (:723-726, :759); it never looks at NoStore, Private or the request's directives, and CompleteNotModifiedRevalidationAsync stores the result (CacheInterceptor.StreamingDispatch.cs:58-63).

**Failure scenario.** A resource was cacheable and is now sensitive: the origin answers the revalidation with 304 and `Cache-Control: no-store, max-age=60`. The entry is rewritten with the new headers and served as a HIT for another 60 s, while a 200 with the same header would have evicted it (test CacheInterceptor_RevalidateModifiedWithNoStore_EvictsOldEntry). A request sent with `Cache-Control: no-store` likewise rewrites the stored entry on a 304.

## Spec reference
RFC 9111 3, 5.2.1.5, 5.2.2.5

## Suggested fix
Run the same storability predicate on the merged headers and the revalidating request; when it fails, serve the stored body for this response and remove the entry (the path at StreamingDispatch.cs:69-70 already exists).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The storability predicate used for 200 responses also runs on the merged headers and the revalidating request
- [ ] When the predicate fails the stored body is served for this response and the entry is removed
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ fails before the fix and passes after it, including a 304 with no-store, max-age=60

title: [Cache] Cache hit and store paths deep-clone header collections repeatedly, allocating per request
body:
## Summary
A cache hit for a response with 15 header fields allocates two dictionaries and about 30 lists plus further small objects, and a stored miss makes five header-collection copies. The hit path is meant to be cheap and runs per request on mobile GCs.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheInterceptor.cs:774`

## Problem
Hit: MemoryCacheStorage.GetAsync deep-clones the entry under the gate (MemoryCacheStorage.cs:64 -> CacheEntry.cs:102, plus a HashSet, array and sort in NormalizeVaryHeaders :206-232); ServeCachedEntryAsync clones the headers again (:774); BufferedResponseBodySource clones the non-null HttpHeaders.Empty trailers (:794, Runtime/Core/Internal/BufferedResponseBodySource.cs:21); a Dictionary is allocated per timeline event (:344); GetSignatureSnapshot runs LINQ OrderBy/ToArray under _indexLock (CacheInterceptor.Variants.cs:160); ParseSignature allocates a char[] and a string[] (:102); the key is built as two strings (CacheInterceptor.UriNormalization.cs:34-41, CacheInterceptor.Variants.cs:107). Store: response headers are deep-cloned five times (CacheStoringHandler.cs:59 even for non-storable statuses, :105 or :215, CacheInterceptor.cs:587, CacheEntry.cs:102, MemoryCacheStorage.cs:205) and request headers twice (CacheStoringHandler.cs:41, :212). Revalidation copies the request headers three times (:428, CopyWithSharedContent and WithHeaders at :434-436). TeeBodySource creates a CancellationTokenSource with a timer on dispose when the consumer never asked for trailers (CacheStoringHandler.cs:388).

**Failure scenario.** A cache hit for a response with 15 header fields allocates two dictionaries and about 30 lists plus a dozen small objects; a stored miss allocates five header-collection copies. The hit path is the one meant to be cheap, and it is paid per request on non-generational mobile GCs.

## Suggested fix
Keep stored headers frozen so GetAsync can return the stored entry and only ServeCachedEntryAsync copies once; pass null trailers when empty; cache the sorted signature array in the bucket; drop the redundant clones in CacheStoringHandler and TeeBodySource; read trailers with CancellationToken.None when the body already reached EOF.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A cache hit copies the stored headers once (in ServeCachedEntryAsync) and the stored entry is returned from GetAsync without cloning; empty trailers are passed as null
- [ ] Redundant clones in CacheStoringHandler and TeeBodySource are removed and the sorted Vary signature array is cached in the bucket
- [ ] Allocations per HIT for a 15-header response are measured before and after and reduced to at most one header-collection copy
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ fails before the fix and passes after it asserting stored entries are not mutated by served responses

title: [Cache] CacheInterceptor always overwrites X-Cache on served entries and the header cannot be disabled
body:
## Summary
Cached responses always get an 'X-Cache: HIT' header that replaces an origin or CDN X-Cache field, and there is no option to turn it off. Apps that read the CDN's X-Cache see the client cache's value only on cached responses.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheInterceptor.cs:777`

## Problem
ServeCachedEntryAsync does headers.Set("X-Cache", provenance) for HIT/STALE/REVALIDATED (CacheInterceptor.cs:774-777). Set replaces any stored value. The header is not mentioned in Documentation~ and there is no CachePolicy switch; RFC 9211 defines Cache-Status for this purpose.

**Failure scenario.** A CDN response stored with 'X-Cache: Hit from cloudfront' is replayed with 'X-Cache: HIT'; app diagnostics that read the CDN's header get the client cache's value on cached responses and the CDN's on network responses.

## Spec reference
RFC 9211

## Suggested fix
Report provenance through RequestContext state/timeline (already recorded) or append an RFC 9211 Cache-Status member; if a header stays, make it opt-in and do not overwrite an existing field.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] An existing X-Cache field from the origin is not overwritten
- [ ] Cache provenance is reported through RequestContext state or timeline, or via an RFC 9211 Cache-Status member; an X-Cache header, if kept, is opt-in
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [Cache] CacheInterceptor.Dispose cancels background work without awaiting it before disposing owned storage
body:
## Summary
Dispose cancels background stores and stale-while-revalidate refreshes but does not wait for them, and there is no way to drain them. Disposing during an in-flight store causes spurious ObjectDisposedException diagnostics from the owned storage, and there is no deterministic quiescent point for app quit, Enter Play Mode without domain reload, or tests.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheInterceptor.cs:841`

## Problem
Dispose cancels the token and immediately disposes the owned MemoryCacheStorage (CacheInterceptor.cs:841-858). Queued mutations and background revalidations (QueueBackgroundWork, 1212-1225) are observed only for logging; there is no DisposeAsync or public drain (PendingMutationCount is an internal test hook, 1232-1241). architecture.md's contract is 'Background work always has an owner that observes its exception and awaits it on dispose'. A mutation already inside Storage.SetAsync/RemoveAsync hits MemoryCacheStorage.ThrowIfDisposed and is logged as 'Store failed' / 'Background revalidation failed'.

**Failure scenario.** Disposing the interceptor while a store or stale-while-revalidate refresh is in flight produces spurious ObjectDisposedException diagnostics from the owned storage, and there is no deterministic point at which the cache is quiescent (app quit, Enter Play Mode without domain reload, tests have to poll the internal PendingMutationCount).

## Suggested fix
Track background tasks and add IAsyncDisposable (or a FlushAsync) that waits for them with a bound; dispose the owned storage only after they have completed.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Background cache tasks are tracked and a bounded drain (IAsyncDisposable or FlushAsync) waits for them
- [ ] Owned storage is disposed only after the background tasks have completed or the bound has elapsed
- [ ] No ObjectDisposedException is surfaced from the storage when disposing during an in-flight store
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [Cache] A GET in flight when an unsafe request invalidates its URL still stores its older response afterwards
body:
## Summary
Invalidation by an unsafe method (RFC 9111 section 4.4) removes the stored key, but a GET that started before it and completes after it still stores its pre-invalidation response. The next GET is a HIT with stale data for the full max-age.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheInterceptor.cs:866`

## Problem
Invalidation removes what is stored at that moment (InvalidateBaseKeyCoreAsync, CacheInterceptor.cs:1071-1083). A store is queued when the GET's body completes (TeeBodySource.DisposeAsync, CacheStoringHandler.cs:327-337; QueueStoreResponse, CacheInterceptor.cs:866-909) and carries the request time, but StoreResponseAsync never compares it with a later invalidation of the same base key (:911-966).

**Failure scenario.** The app sends GET /inventory and, before its body has finished, POST /inventory/use. The POST's 200 invalidates the (empty) key; the GET then completes and stores the pre-POST representation with max-age=300. The next GET /inventory is a HIT with the old inventory for five minutes: the section 4.4 invalidation had no effect.

## Spec reference
RFC 9111 4.4

## Suggested fix
Keep a per-base-key invalidation timestamp (or generation) and drop a store whose request time precedes it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each base key records an invalidation timestamp or generation and a store whose request time precedes it is dropped
- [ ] A GET that began after the invalidation still stores normally
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ fails before the fix and passes after it with a GET in flight across a POST invalidation

title: [Cache] CacheStoringHandler copies every candidate response body before the header-only storability decision
body:
## Summary
Every 2xx GET body is copied into pooled segments while it is read and then into a full-size byte[] (LOH above 85 KB) before the storability decision, even when the response can never be stored, such as an API without Cache-Control under the default policy. Non-storable responses pay the full copy cost.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheInterceptor.cs:940`

## Problem
CacheStoringHandler.OnResponseStartAsync gates only on status, null body and Length (CacheStoringHandler.cs:60-76). It then either copies the buffered body into a new SegmentedBuffer (:105-111) or wraps the body in TeeBodySource, whose Accumulate copies every read into pooled 16 KB segments (:147-160, :357-378) and which answers TryDetachBufferedBody with false (:233-237), disabling the transport's zero-copy detach. StoreResponseAsync flattens that to a new byte[] (CacheInterceptor.cs:940-942) and only afterwards calls PrepareEntryForStorage (:943-955), whose rejections depend on headers alone: Set-Cookie (:590), Authorization (:596), no-store (:603), private (:606), Vary (:609-618), no freshness with the default DoNotCacheWithoutFreshness=true (:631-641). MemoryCacheStorage.SetAsync additionally drops entries above its maxSizeBytes after the copy (MemoryCacheStorage.cs:95-96).

**Failure scenario.** Client with CacheInterceptor talking to an API that sends no Cache-Control/Expires (never stored under the default policy): every GET 2xx body is memcpy'd into pooled segments while it is read, then a thread-pool item allocates a byte[] of the full body size (LOH above 85 KB, up to 8 MiB), copies the body again and discards it. Two extra body copies and one body-sized garbage array per request for no cache benefit, on GCs (Mono/IL2CPP Boehm) that do not compact.

## Suggested fix
Run the header-only part of PrepareEntryForStorage in CacheStoringHandler.OnResponseStartAsync (and clamp to the storage size limit when it is known) and pass the body through untouched when the response cannot be stored. When Content-Length is known, accumulate straight into one exact-size owned byte[] instead of SegmentedBuffer plus ToArray.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The header-only part of PrepareEntryForStorage runs in CacheStoringHandler.OnResponseStartAsync and non-storable responses are passed through without tee or buffering
- [ ] When Content-Length is known the body is accumulated into one exact-size owned byte[] and the size is clamped to the storage limit
- [ ] Allocations and copies per non-storable 2xx response are measured and reduced to zero extra body copies
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `cache-runtime-01` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/cache.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: performance.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. CacheStoringHandler.OnResponseStartAsync gates only on ShouldConsiderForStorage (status/method), null body and Length (Runtime/Cache/CacheStoringHandler.cs:60-76), then copies a buffered body into a new SegmentedBuffer (:105-111) or wraps the body in TeeBodySource, whose Accumulate copies every read (:252, :357-378). StoreResponseAsync flattens with body.AsSequence().ToArray() (CacheInterceptor.cs:940-942) before PrepareEntryForStorage (:943-953), whose rejections are header-only (:590, :596-618, :631-641); MemoryCacheStorage can still drop the entry afterwards (MemoryCacheStorage.cs:95-96). So with the default DoNotCacheWithoutFreshness=true every GET 2xx without freshness pays two body copies and one body-sized array for nothing. Minor correction: the lost zero-copy detach (:233-237) matters only where the inner source can detach (HTTP/2 or buffered sources); Http11ResponseBodySource.TryDetachBufferedBody succeeds only for empty bodies (Http11ResponseBodySource.cs:99-121). Cost applies only to clients that install CacheInterceptor.

Also reported as `cache-design-08` (merged into this issue).

Related: [[R11-cache-runtime-12]].

title: [Cache] CacheInterceptor calls ICacheStorage synchronously while holding the global _pendingMutationLock for four mutation kinds
body:
## Summary
304 merges, post-revalidation removals and invalidations invoke the storage inline under the single global lock. A custom store that does synchronous I/O before returning a completed Task stalls all cache lookups and stores for every key.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheInterceptor.cs:1106`

## Problem
QueueMutationAsync calls RunQueuedMutationAsync inside lock(_pendingMutationLock) (CacheInterceptor.cs:1106-1111); with no previous task the mutation delegate runs inline up to its first incomplete await (1178-1197). StoreResponseAsync and RemoveEvictedVariantsCoreAsync leave the lock first with 'await new ThreadPoolHop()' and say why (924-928, Variants.cs:262-263). StorePreparedEntryCoreAsync (1039-1048), ReplaceStoredEntryCoreAsync (1050-1060), RemoveStoredEntryCoreAsync (1062-1069) and InvalidateBaseKeyCoreAsync (1071-1083) do not hop, so Storage.SetAsync/RemoveAsync run their synchronous part under the lock, plus _indexLock nested inside it. Every cacheable GET takes the same lock in AwaitPendingMutationAsync (1130-1133).

**Failure scenario.** A custom store whose SetAsync/RemoveAsync does synchronous file I/O before returning a completed Task: each 304 merge, post-revalidation removal and POST invalidation performs that I/O while holding the lock, stalling every concurrent cache lookup and store for all keys for the duration of the disk operation.

## Suggested fix
Start mutations outside the lock (reserve the queue slot with a TaskCompletionSource under the lock, run the mutation after releasing it), or apply the same hop to all mutation bodies; document that storage is never called under an interceptor lock.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Mutations start outside _pendingMutationLock (queue slot reserved under the lock, mutation run after release) for all mutation kinds
- [ ] Documented and tested that ICacheStorage is never called under an interceptor lock
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ fails before the fix and passes after it using a storage that blocks inside SetAsync/RemoveAsync

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `cache-design-07` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/cache.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: low. Angle: architecture.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: QueueMutationAsync calls RunQueuedMutationAsync inside lock(_pendingMutationLock) (CacheInterceptor.cs:1106-1111); with no previous task or a completed one it runs the mutation inline up to its first incomplete await (:1178-1197). StoreResponseAsync (:928) and RemoveEvictedVariantsCoreAsync (Variants.cs:263) hop first and say why; StorePreparedEntryCoreAsync, ReplaceStoredEntryCoreAsync, RemoveStoredEntryCoreAsync and InvalidateBaseKeyCoreAsync (:1039-1083) do not, so the synchronous part of Storage.SetAsync/RemoveAsync runs under the lock, and RegisterStoredVariant then nests _indexLock. With MemoryCacheStorage that synchronous part can be the whole SetAsync, including the expiry sweep, when the gate is free (MemoryCacheStorage.cs:81-119). No lock inversion found (QueueEvictedVariantRemoval runs outside _indexLock, Variants.cs:195-196). Low: for the shipped storage this is microseconds of in-memory work over at most MaxEntries items; real stalls need a custom store that does blocking I/O before its first await.

Also reported as `cache-runtime-09` (merged into this issue).

title: [Cache] With CacheInterceptor outside RedirectInterceptor, the final response of a redirect chain is stored under the original URL
body:
## Summary
CacheStoringHandler keys the stored response by the URI captured before inner interceptors run. With Interceptors = [CacheInterceptor, RedirectInterceptor] the final response from the redirect target is stored under the original request's key, so later requests to the original URL get another origin's content.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheStoringHandler.cs:40`

## Problem
CacheStoringHandler captures `_requestUri = request.Uri` and the base key of the request the cache saw (CacheStoringHandler.cs:39-42; created at CacheInterceptor.cs:388-392) and ignores the request passed to OnRequestStart (:48-51). An inner RedirectInterceptor consumes the 3xx and re-dispatches with the same handler chain (Runtime/Middleware/RedirectHandler.cs:237-242), then forwards only the final response to `_inner` (:147), i.e. to CacheStoringHandler, which stores it with base key and ResponseUrl of the first URL (QueueStoreResponse, CacheStoringHandler.cs:125-135; StoreResponseAsync passes requestUri as responseUrl, CacheInterceptor.cs:952). InterceptorOrdering rejects only Cache-outside-Auth and Concurrency-outside-Retry (Runtime/Core/Pipeline/InterceptorOrdering.cs:53-70); Documentation~/Modules/Interceptors.md lists Redirect first as canonical but does not forbid the other order. No cache test involves a redirect.

**Failure scenario.** Interceptors = [CacheInterceptor, RedirectInterceptor]. GET https://api.example/session answers 302 to https://cdn.example/login.html, which answers 200 with max-age=86400. The login page is stored under 'GET https://api.example/session'. For the next 24 h that URL is a HIT with the CDN page: the temporary redirect, which carried no freshness and is not cacheable by default, has effectively been cached for the target's lifetime, across origins; a POST to the target does not invalidate it (section 4.4 keys differ). The same happens on the revalidation path through CompleteModifiedRevalidationAsync.

## Spec reference
RFC 9111 2, 3, 4.4; RFC 9110 15.4.3

## Suggested fix
In CacheStoringHandler.OnRequestStart compare the effective request (the one forwarded by inner interceptors) with the captured URI and skip the store when the target URI changed, or key the store by the effective URI; alternatively add a Cache-outside-Redirect rule to InterceptorOrdering. Add a test with a redirect inside the cache.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The store is skipped or keyed by the effective URI when the request URI changed between the lookup and CacheStoringHandler.OnRequestStart
- [ ] A redirect chain through RedirectInterceptor never stores the target response under the original URL's key
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ fails before the fix and passes after it with a redirect inside the cache

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `cache-protocol-06` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/cache.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: protocol-impl.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. CacheStoringHandler captures request.Uri and the base key of the request the cache saw (Runtime/Cache/CacheStoringHandler.cs:39-42) and OnRequestStart ignores the effective request (:48-51). With [CacheInterceptor, RedirectInterceptor], RedirectHandler consumes the 3xx, re-dispatches with itself as handler (Runtime/Middleware/RedirectHandler.cs:237-242) and forwards only the final non-redirect response to _inner (:147), i.e. CacheStoringHandler, which stores it under the first URL's key with requestUri as ResponseUrl (CacheInterceptor.cs:943-953). InterceptorOrdering has only the Cache-outside-Auth and Concurrency-outside-Retry rules (Runtime/Core/Pipeline/InterceptorOrdering.cs:53-70); the docs list Redirect above Cache as canonical (Documentation~/Modules/Interceptors.md:51-62) but neither reject nor warn about the reverse, and no cache test involves a redirect. Consequence: a temporary redirect (e.g. /latest -> versioned immutable asset) is pinned for the target's freshness lifetime and later GETs never re-evaluate the redirect. Requires the non-canonical but accepted order.

Also reported as `cache-design-02` (merged into this issue).

title: [Cache] Authorization and Vary guards use the pre-interceptor request, so credentials added by inner interceptors bypass them
body:
## Summary
The cache decides storability and the Vary key from the request as it was at the cache's pipeline position. Authorization, Cookie or API-key headers added by any interceptor placed after the cache are invisible, so AllowCacheForAuthorizedRequests=false does not apply and a per-user response can be stored under a user-less key and served to others.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheStoringHandler.cs:41`

## Problem
CacheStoringHandler snapshots `request.Headers.Clone()` in its constructor (CacheStoringHandler.cs:41) and its OnRequestStart discards the effective request the transport reports (:48-51). PrepareEntryForStorage applies the RFC 9111 section 3.5 guard (`requestHeaders.Contains("Authorization")`, CacheInterceptor.cs:596-601) and builds the Vary key (:647) from that snapshot; lookups do the same with request.Headers (:542). The pipeline only rejects Cache outside the first-party AuthInterceptor (InterceptorOrdering.cs:53-62); DefaultHeadersInterceptor, CookieInterceptor and every user-written interceptor have role None (InterceptorOrdering.cs:72-75), so they are accepted inside the cache.

**Failure scenario.** A project adds its own token interceptor (or DefaultHeadersInterceptor with an Authorization/X-Api-Key header) after CacheInterceptor. The cache never sees Authorization, so AllowCacheForAuthorizedRequests=false does not apply: GET /me with `max-age=60` is stored under a user-less key and, after the user logs out and another logs in (or a second client shares the CacheInterceptor, as the docs suggest), the first user's response is served as a HIT. With CookieInterceptor inside the cache and AllowVaryCookie=true, `Vary: Cookie` variants all get the key `cookie=~` and are shared across cookie states; a language header added by an inner DefaultHeadersInterceptor makes `Vary: Accept-Language` variants collide the same way.

## Spec reference
RFC 9111 3.5, 4.1

## Suggested fix
Take the request headers used for the Authorization guard, the request no-store check and the Vary key from the request delivered to CacheStoringHandler.OnRequestStart (the effective request), and refuse to store when a Vary-nominated header differs between the lookup-time and the effective request. Document that custom credential interceptors must sit outside the cache.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The Authorization guard, request no-store check and Vary key use the effective request delivered to CacheStoringHandler.OnRequestStart
- [ ] Storage is refused when a Vary-nominated header differs between the lookup-time and the effective request
- [ ] Documentation states that credential interceptors must sit outside the cache
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ fails before the fix and passes after it with a header-adding interceptor after the cache

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `cache-protocol-07` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/cache.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: security.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. The storability guard `requestHeaders.Contains("Authorization")` (Runtime/Cache/CacheInterceptor.cs:596-601), the request no-store check (:603) and the Vary key (:647, lookup :542) all use the header snapshot taken in CacheStoringHandler's constructor (Runtime/Cache/CacheStoringHandler.cs:41); the effective request delivered to OnRequestStart is discarded (:48-51). The #55 guard covers only the first-party AuthInterceptor (InterceptorOrdering.cs:53-62): DefaultHeadersInterceptor declares no role (Runtime/Middleware/DefaultHeadersInterceptor.cs:13) and adds headers on a copy passed to next (:44-52), as would CookieInterceptor and any user interceptor (GetRole -> None, InterceptorOrdering.cs:72-75). So an Authorization/API-key header added inside the cache bypasses AllowCacheForAuthorizedRequests=false and Vary variants collapse onto the `~` key. The documented trade-off's guard is incomplete, not wrong; exploitation needs a non-canonical order (docs only state the Auth-above-Cache rule, Documentation~/Modules/Auth.md:18). Related to but not covered by #117 step 2 (partition key). Shares its root cause (ignored effective request) with cache-protocol-06 but is a distinct defect.

Also reported as `cache-design-01` (merged into this issue).

Related: #117, [[R11-cache-protocol-06]].

title: [Cache] TeeBodySource commits a truncated or empty body after GetTrailersAsync drains the inner source
body:
## Summary
TeeBodySource treats any 0-byte read from the inner source as natural end of stream. When a consumer calls GetTrailersAsync before reading the body, the HTTP/1.1 body source drains the unread body internally, bypassing the tee's accumulator, and the next read returns 0. The tee then stores the response headers with an empty or prefix-only body, and later requests are served that truncated body as a cache hit for the whole freshness lifetime.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheStoringHandler.cs:246`

## Problem
TeeBodySource.ReadAsync sets `_completedNaturally` whenever the inner read returns 0 (CacheStoringHandler.cs:245-250). Http11ResponseBodySource.ReadAsync returns 0 for an empty destination without being at EOF (Runtime/Transport/Http1/Http11ResponseBodySource.cs:129-130; Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:195-196 likewise). TeeBodySource.GetTrailersAsync forwards to the inner source (:299), and the HTTP/1.1 source then drains the unread body internally (Http11ResponseBodySource.cs:267-274, DrainThenReturnEmptyAsync/DrainThenGetTrailersAsync), bypassing Accumulate; a later ReadAsync returns 0 and marks natural completion. DisposeAsync commits when not aborted, `_completedNaturally` is set and trailers are loaded (:316-337); EnsureTrailersLoadedForStoreAsync also calls the draining GetTrailersAsync (:389). Nothing compares `_accumulatedBytes` with `_inner.Length`. Tests cover natural EOF and dispose-before-EOF only (CacheInterceptorTests.Streaming.cs).

**Failure scenario.** Streaming GET over HTTP/1.1 of a cacheable 200 (max-age=600, Content-Length 100000). The consumer calls `await response.GetTrailersAsync()` first (documented as allowed before EOF, UHttpStreamingResponse.cs:63-75), then reads the body stream to the end (gets 0 immediately) and disposes. The tee stores an entry with the 200's headers and an empty (or prefix-only) body; every request for the next 10 minutes is a HIT with that truncated body. A handler-level consumer that issues one zero-length ReadAsync and then disposes early gets the same result through EnsureTrailersLoadedForStoreAsync.

## Spec reference
RFC 9111 3.3

## Suggested fix
Do not treat a 0 result for an empty destination as EOF; when trailers are requested before natural EOF, either drain through the tee's own ReadAsync or detach the accumulator; before committing require `_accumulatedBytes == _inner.Length` when the length is known. Add regression tests for both sequences.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A 0-byte read for an empty destination buffer is not treated as natural end of stream by TeeBodySource
- [ ] When trailers are requested before end of stream, the tee either accumulates the drained bytes or detaches the accumulator so no truncated entry is stored
- [ ] Before committing, the tee requires accumulated bytes to equal the inner source length when that length is known
- [ ] Regression tests cover both sequences (GetTrailersAsync before reading, and a zero-length read followed by dispose) under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ and fail before the fix

## Context

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced for the trailers-first sequence through the public API. TeeBodySource.GetTrailersAsync forwards to the inner source (Runtime/Cache/CacheStoringHandler.cs:299); Http11ResponseBodySource.GetTrailersAsync drains the unread body itself when not terminal (Runtime/Transport/Http1/Http11ResponseBodySource.cs:267-274, 438-448), bypassing Accumulate. The next read returns 0 because _terminalState == 1 (:132-133), the tee sets _completedNaturally (CacheStoringHandler.cs:246-249) and ResponseBodyStream flags end of stream (Runtime/Core/ResponseBodyStream.cs:164-170), so UHttpStreamingResponse.Dispose takes the DisposeAsync path (UHttpStreamingResponse.cs:157-166) and the tee commits an empty or prefix-only accumulator (CacheStoringHandler.cs:316-337). The trigger is an unusual consumer sequence, but the result is a truncated entry served as HIT to later correct consumers for the whole freshness lifetime.

title: [Cache] TeeBodySource.Abort and DisposeAsync return pooled accumulator segments while a concurrent ReadAsync may still be writing into them
body:
## Summary
TeeBodySource.ReadAsync copies each chunk into a SegmentedBuffer that is not thread-safe, while Abort and DisposeAsync dispose that buffer and return its segments to ArrayPool without excluding an in-flight write. UHttpStreamingResponse.Dispose calls Abort from the caller's thread when end of stream was not reached, which is the case where a read loop can be running on another thread. A segment can be returned to the pool while still being written, corrupting another request's buffer, or the write fails with an exception.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/CacheStoringHandler.cs:281`

## Problem
ReadAsync calls Accumulate on the reader thread after the inner read returns (:245-253). Accumulate reads _accumulator without synchronisation and calls _accumulator.Write (:359-371), which memcpy's into the tail PooledSegment of a SegmentedBuffer documented as not thread-safe (Core/Internal/SegmentedBuffer.cs:26, 66-85). Abort() (:281-288) and the finally of DisposeAsync (:352) call Interlocked.Exchange(ref _accumulator, null)?.Dispose(), i.e. SegmentedBuffer.Dispose -> ReturnAllSegments -> ByteArrayPool.Return (SegmentedBuffer.cs:186-193, 219-228), with nothing excluding an in-flight Accumulate. UHttpStreamingResponse.Dispose() calls _bodySource.Abort() from the caller's thread whenever EOF was not reached (Core/UHttpStreamingResponse.cs:157-161), which is exactly the case where a read loop can be running on another thread.

**Failure scenario.** A pool thread is inside Accumulate copying a chunk of a cacheable streamed download; the main thread disposes the UHttpStreamingResponse (OnDestroy, user cancel). Abort returns the segment arrays to ArrayPool while the copy still writes into them; a request that rents one of those arrays in that window has its buffer overwritten with this response's bytes. More often it shows up as a NullReferenceException/ArgumentOutOfRangeException inside Write that the catch at :373 logs as 'Tee accumulator detached after write failure'.

## Suggested fix
Give the accumulator a single owner: Abort/DisposeAsync should only mark it abandoned (or take a small lock shared with Accumulate) and the reader thread, or DisposeAsync once no read is in flight, returns the segments.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The accumulator has a single owner: Abort and DisposeAsync mark it abandoned or take a lock shared with Accumulate, and the segments are returned exactly once after no write is in flight
- [ ] Disposing the streaming response during a concurrent read never returns a segment that is still being written and never logs 'Tee accumulator detached after write failure' for this case
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ that overlaps Abort with an in-flight Accumulate fails before the fix

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `cache-runtime-02` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/cache.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: concurrency.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced: no lock or single owner. Accumulate runs on the reader thread after the inner read (Runtime/Cache/CacheStoringHandler.cs:245-253), reads _accumulator without synchronisation and calls Write (:359-371), which copies into the tail PooledSegment of a SegmentedBuffer documented as not thread-safe (Runtime/Core/Internal/SegmentedBuffer.cs:26, 66-85). Abort (:281-288 -> DetachAccumulator :410-413) and DisposeAsync's finally (:352) exchange the field and Dispose the accumulator, i.e. SegmentedBuffer.Dispose -> ReturnAllSegments (SegmentedBuffer.cs:186-193, 219-228), with nothing excluding an in-flight Write. UHttpStreamingResponse.Dispose calls _bodySource.Abort() from the caller's thread when EOF was not reached (Runtime/Core/UHttpStreamingResponse.cs:157-161) and ResponseBodyStream dispose does the same (ResponseBodyStream.cs:181-187); the inner sources' Abort is CAS-based and meant to be called concurrently with a read, and the tee's own Interlocked flags show the same intent. Result when the dispose lands inside the copy: a segment is returned to ByteArrayPool while still being written (cross-request buffer corruption if re-rented in that window), or an NRE/ObjectDisposedException caught at :373. The window is one memcpy of at most 16 KB, so it is rare, but the dispose-during-read pattern (main thread OnDestroy vs pool-thread read) is ordinary in Unity.

title: [Cache] ICacheStorage requires ClearAsync, GetCountAsync and GetSizeAsync that the interceptor never calls, and CacheInterceptor has no way to invalidate one URL
body:
## Summary
ICacheStorage declares ClearAsync, GetCountAsync and GetSizeAsync, which nothing in Runtime calls except MemoryCacheStorage itself, while the storage key format is private and CacheInterceptor exposes no invalidation API. An application that wants to drop one cached URL can only wipe the whole cache. Custom storage authors must implement accounting that is never used.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/ICacheStorage.cs:28`

## Problem
ClearAsync, GetCountAsync and GetSizeAsync (ICacheStorage.cs:28-41) have no caller in Runtime outside MemoryCacheStorage (rg over Runtime); only tests call them. CacheInterceptor exposes no ClearAsync/InvalidateAsync(Uri); keys are built by private BuildBaseKey/BuildStorageKey ('GET <normalized-uri>|<vary-key>', Variants.cs:105-113) and NormalizeUri is internal (UriNormalization.cs:16). SetAsync takes both key and entry although entry.Key always equals key (MemoryCacheStorage.EnsureKey, 202-222, exists only for that redundancy). The interface docs still say 'cache middleware'.

**Failure scenario.** An app needs to drop the cached profile response after an in-app purchase confirmed over WebSocket: there is no public API to compute the storage key or invalidate by URL, so the only option is storage.ClearAsync(), wiping the whole cache; a custom store author must implement size/count accounting that nothing uses.

## Suggested fix
Add InvalidateAsync(Uri)/ClearAsync to CacheInterceptor (routed through the mutation queue and the variant index) and move count/size to an optional diagnostics interface.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] CacheInterceptor exposes a public InvalidateAsync(Uri) and ClearAsync that go through the mutation queue and the variant index
- [ ] Count and size members move to an optional diagnostics interface, so a minimal ICacheStorage implements only get, set and remove
- [ ] XML docs describe the new API and the contract is mentioned in the PR
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ shows InvalidateAsync removes all variants of one URL and leaves other URLs cached

title: [Docs] Public members of MemoryCacheStorage, CacheEntry, CacheInterceptor, RetryInterceptor and ConcurrencyInterceptor lack XML docs; ICacheStorage docs say 'middleware'

## Summary
Several public members in the Cache, Retry and RateLimit modules have no XML documentation, including the MemoryCacheStorage constructor and its default limits. ICacheStorage's docs still say 'cache middleware' and do not state whether GetAsync may return a shared instance, whether SetAsync may keep the passed entry, or whether the store may evict on expiry. A custom storage author cannot tell the ownership and cloning contract from the code documentation.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/MemoryCacheStorage.cs:36`

## Problem
No XML docs on: MemoryCacheStorage constructor (defaults 100 entries / 10 MiB, line 36) and its public methods and Dispose (50-200); CacheEntry.Clone (CacheEntry.cs:176); CacheInterceptor.Wrap and Dispose (CacheInterceptor.cs:295, 841); RetryInterceptor.Wrap (RetryInterceptor.cs:31) and its 'log' parameter; ConcurrencyInterceptor.Wrap and Dispose (ConcurrencyInterceptor.cs:48, 74). Document the listed members and state the ICacheStorage ownership, cloning and eviction contract explicitly.

title: [Cache] MemoryCacheStorage expiry sweep evicts stale entries that still have ETag/Last-Modified validators, defeating conditional revalidation
body:
## Summary
MemoryCacheStorage sweeps expired entries every 15 seconds on store and forces a sweep when full, and CacheEntry.ShouldEvict ignores whether the entry can be revalidated. The interceptor needs the stale entry to send If-None-Match, and the ICacheStorage contract says expiry decisions belong to the interceptor. In an app with steady cacheable traffic, entries with max-age and an ETag are removed before revalidation, so EnableRevalidation rarely saves a body.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/MemoryCacheStorage.cs:92`

## Problem
SetAsync calls MaybeSweepExpiredEntriesUnsafe on every store once 15 s have passed since the last sweep (MemoryCacheStorage.cs:17, 92, 280-287), and GetCountAsync/GetSizeAsync force it (169, 185). RemoveExpiredEntriesUnsafe removes every entry whose CacheEntry.ShouldEvict is true (267-278); ShouldEvict (CacheEntry.cs:164-174) is true as soon as now >= ExpiresAtUtc outside a stale-while-revalidate window and does not look at CanRevalidate(). ICacheStorage's contract says the opposite: 'Expiry/revalidation decisions are handled by cache middleware' (ICacheStorage.cs:13-15), and the interceptor's own path keeps a stale entry to send If-None-Match (CacheInterceptor.cs:365-376). The sweep uses DateTime.UtcNow while the interceptor uses its _utcNow seam, so the fake-clock tests never exercise it. Entries without ExpiresAtUtc (no-cache + ETag) are never swept, so behaviour is also inconsistent between 'no-cache' and 'max-age=0'.

**Failure scenario.** A is stored with 'Cache-Control: max-age=60' and an ETag. At t=70 s any other response is stored: the sweep removes A. At t=80 s GET A is a plain miss and downloads the full body instead of a conditional request answered by 304. With the common 'max-age=0' + ETag pattern the entry is removed by the first store that runs 15 s later, so EnableRevalidation rarely saves a body in an app with steady cacheable traffic.

## Spec reference
RFC 9111 section 4.3

## Suggested fix
Do not evict on freshness in the storage: rely on the LRU/size bounds, or evict only expired entries that cannot be revalidated (no ETag/Last-Modified). If a sweep stays, drive it from the interceptor's clock and policy.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] MemoryCacheStorage does not evict expired entries that can be revalidated (have ETag or Last-Modified); it relies on the LRU and size bounds for them
- [ ] Any sweep that remains uses the interceptor's clock and policy rather than DateTime.UtcNow
- [ ] Behaviour is consistent between 'no-cache' with a validator and 'max-age=0' with a validator
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ stores an entry with max-age and ETag, advances a fake clock past the sweep interval, stores another entry, and asserts the stale entry is still returned for conditional revalidation

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `cache-design-03` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/cache.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: architecture.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: CacheEntry.ShouldEvict (Runtime/Cache/CacheEntry.cs:164-174) returns true once now >= ExpiresAtUtc outside a stale-while-revalidate window and never consults CanRevalidate(). MemoryCacheStorage.SetAsync calls MaybeSweepExpiredEntriesUnsafe with DateTime.UtcNow (MemoryCacheStorage.cs:87-92; interval 15 s at :17, :280-287), forces it when full (:99-100) and in GetCountAsync/GetSizeAsync (:169, :185); RemoveExpiredEntriesUnsafe removes every such entry (:267-278). The interceptor's conditional revalidation needs the expired entry returned by GetAsync (CacheInterceptor.cs:365-376), and the ICacheStorage contract says expiry decisions belong to the middleware (ICacheStorage.cs:13-15). A 304 merge is itself a SetAsync (CacheInterceptor.cs:1039-1047), so one revalidation sweeps every other expired validator-bearing entry. No test contradicts this: CacheInterceptor_RevalidatesExpiredEntries_ThatHaveValidators (Tests/Runtime/Cache/CacheInterceptorTests.VariantsAndAsync.cs:306-349) does two back-to-back requests, inside the 15 s interval, and nothing under Tests/Runtime exercises the sweep. Entries without ExpiresAtUtc (no-cache + validator) are never swept (CacheEntry.cs:166-167), so the behaviour is inconsistent. RFC 9111 does not require keeping stale entries, so this is cache-efficacy loss, not a protocol violation.

Also reported as `cache-runtime-06` (merged into this issue).

title: [Cache] MemoryCacheStorage at capacity scans every entry for expiry on each insert
body:
## Summary
When MemoryCacheStorage is at its entry or size limit, every SetAsync forces RemoveExpiredEntriesUnsafe, which walks the whole LRU list with a dictionary lookup per node, and then evicts from the tail. A full cache is the steady state of a bounded cache, so each store costs O(n) under the storage gate. With large maxEntries this adds latency to every insert and holds the lock used by 304 merges.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/MemoryCacheStorage.cs:99`

## Problem
When the entry count is at _maxEntries or the size limit would be exceeded, SetAsync forces RemoveExpiredEntriesUnsafe (:99-100), which walks the whole LRU list with a dictionary lookup per node (:267-278), and then evicts from the tail. A full cache is the steady state of a bounded cache.

**Failure scenario.** MemoryCacheStorage(maxEntries: 10000) at capacity: every newly stored key scans 10 000 entries under the storage gate (and, for 304 merges, under the interceptor's _pendingMutationLock, see cache-runtime-09).

## Suggested fix
Rely on the 15 s periodic sweep plus plain LRU eviction under pressure, or keep an expiry-ordered structure so the forced sweep is not O(n) per insert.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Inserting into a full MemoryCacheStorage performs no full scan; it uses the periodic sweep plus LRU eviction, or an expiry-ordered structure
- [ ] The measurable target is O(1) amortized work per insert at capacity, shown by a test that counts visited nodes with 10 000 entries
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ covers eviction at capacity

title: [Cache] MemoryCacheStorage.Dispose disposes its SemaphoreSlim under in-flight operations, so Release throws and queued waiters never complete
body:
## Summary
MemoryCacheStorage guards synchronous sections that contain no await with a SemaphoreSlim, and Dispose disposes it without excluding in-flight operations. SemaphoreSlim.Release throws ObjectDisposedException after disposal and queued async waiters are dropped without being completed. Disposing UHttpClient while requests contend on the storage can make the holder throw over its result and leave a waiting request hanging.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/MemoryCacheStorage.cs:199`

## Problem
Every operation takes _gate with WaitAsync although the guarded sections contain no await (:57-69, :84-123). Dispose() disposes the gate without excluding in-flight operations (:194-200). SemaphoreSlim.Release throws ObjectDisposedException after Dispose, and Dispose drops queued async waiters without completing them.

**Failure scenario.** UHttpClient.Dispose() (owned storage) while two requests contend on the gate: the holder's finally { _gate.Release(); } throws ObjectDisposedException over its result, and the queued waiter's WaitAsync task is never completed, so that request hangs unless its own token is cancelled (the request timeout is not running yet at this point). Confirm with a stress test that disposes during contended Get/Set on Mono and IL2CPP.

## Suggested fix
Guard the dictionary and LRU list with a plain lock and return completed tasks; Dispose then only flips the flag.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] MemoryCacheStorage guards its dictionary and LRU list with a plain lock and returns completed tasks, and Dispose only sets a disposed flag
- [ ] Operations after or during Dispose complete or fail deterministically with ObjectDisposedException and never hang
- [ ] A stress test under Tests/Runtime/Cache/ disposes during contended Get/Set and fails before the fix; confirmed on Mono and IL2CPP

title: [Cache] Cache background work depends on ThreadPool work items and foreground lookups wait for it, which would hang on a thread-less WebGL player
body:
## Summary
Cache stores, variant removals and background revalidation start with ThreadPoolHop, and foreground lookups of the same key wait for the pending store. TurboHTTP.Cache.asmdef does not exclude WebGL, and RetryInterceptor uses Task.Delay. On a player without threads, the queued continuation may never run and the next request for the same URL waits forever. This is not reachable on today's supported targets and becomes relevant with the planned WebGL transport.

## Location
- `Runtime/Cache/ThreadPoolHop.cs:39`

## Problem
Cache stores, evicted-variant removals and background revalidation start with await new ThreadPoolHop() (CacheInterceptor.cs:479, :928; CacheInterceptor.Variants.cs:263), which queues the continuation with ThreadPool.(Unsafe)QueueUserWorkItem (ThreadPoolHop.cs:27-40). Foreground lookups of the same key wait for the pending store (CacheInterceptor.cs:532, 1127-1156). TurboHTTP.Cache.asmdef does not exclude WebGL, and RetryInterceptor waits with Task.Delay (RetryInterceptor.cs:113).

**Failure scenario.** When the planned WebGL fetch transport (#130) is combined with CacheInterceptor on a player without threads, the queued store continuation may never run; the next request for the same URL then waits forever in AwaitPendingMutationAsync. Confirm by running the cache tests in a WebGL player; not reachable on today's supported targets.

## Suggested fix
Before #130 ships, either exclude these modules from WebGL or route the hop through a platform scheduler, and record the dependency on #130.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Before the WebGL transport (#130) ships, the Cache module is excluded from WebGL or ThreadPoolHop routes through a platform scheduler

title: [Architecture] RateLimit, Retry and Cache depend on Core through InternalsVisibleTo; the internal IInterceptorRole marker leaves third-party and wrapping interceptors unordered
body:
## Summary
Core grants InternalsVisibleTo to Cache, Retry and RateLimit, and RateLimit needs it only for the internal IInterceptorRole marker. Because the marker is internal, a third-party or wrapping interceptor has role None and the interceptor ordering rules never apply to it. A user wrapping CacheInterceptor in their own interceptor can place it outside AuthInterceptor without the rejected combination being detected.

## Location
- `Runtime/RateLimit/ConcurrencyInterceptor.cs:17`

## Problem
Core/AssemblyInfo.cs grants IVT to Cache, Retry and RateLimit. Cache uses SegmentedBuffer, ByteArrayPool, BufferedResponseBodySource, TurboDiagnostics, RequestContext.CreateForBackground, UHttpRequest.CopyWithSharedContent and IInterceptorRole; Retry uses ResponseBodyDiscardHelper, BackoffJitter and IInterceptorRole; RateLimit uses only IInterceptorRole/InterceptorRole (ConcurrencyInterceptor.cs:17-20), which #76's list predates. Because the marker is internal (Core/Pipeline/InterceptorOrdering.cs:10-26), a third-party or wrapping interceptor has role None and the #55 ordering rules never apply to it (see cache-design-01).

**Failure scenario.** A user wraps CacheInterceptor in their own IHttpInterceptor (per-host enable switch) and places it outside AuthInterceptor: construction succeeds and the rejected combination runs. The modules cannot be versioned apart from Core.

## Suggested fix
Fold into #76: make the role declaration public (or replace it with structural checks in the modules) and promote the few primitives these modules need.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The interceptor role declaration is public (or replaced by structural checks in the modules) so wrapping interceptors can declare a role
- [ ] RateLimit no longer needs InternalsVisibleTo from Core
- [ ] The ordering rules apply to a wrapped CacheInterceptor and reject the Auth ordering violation

title: [RateLimit] ConcurrencyInterceptor permit wait has no queue bound and is not covered by the request Timeout
body:
## Summary
ConcurrencyInterceptor awaits ConcurrencyLimiter.AcquireAsync with only the caller's token, while the request timeout starts later inside the transport. ConcurrencyLimiter has no queue length or wait limit. When a host stops answering, later requests wait about (N/6) times the timeout before being sent and the queue grows without bound.

## Location
- `Runtime/RateLimit/ConcurrencyInterceptor.cs:60`

## Problem
The interceptor awaits _limiter.AcquireAsync(host, cancellationToken) with the caller's token only (:60). The request timeout starts later, inside the transport (Runtime/Transport/RawSocketTransport.cs:440, CancelAfter(request.Timeout)). The UI keeps issuing requests without a CancellationToken: request N waits roughly (N/6) x timeout before it is even sent, far beyond its own Timeout, and the queue (request, context and handler chain per waiter) grows without bound.

## Suggested fix
Add an optional maximum queue length and/or maximum wait to ConcurrencyLimiter that fails fast with a UHttpException, and document that Timeout does not cover the permit wait.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] ConcurrencyLimiter supports an optional maximum queue length and/or maximum wait that fails fast with a UHttpException of a documented UHttpError
- [ ] The docs state that Timeout does not cover the permit wait unless the limit is configured

title: [RateLimit] ConcurrencyLimiter and RequestQueue allocate a linked CancellationTokenSource per acquire even when a permit is free

AcquireAsync creates and disposes a linked CancellationTokenSource, registering on a CTS shared by all requests, before trying the semaphores. Try Wait(0) on both semaphores first (and a non-waiting dequeue in the queue) and build the linked token only when a wait is needed.

title: [RateLimit] ConcurrencyLimiter takes the global permit before the per-host permit, so queued requests for one saturated host block all other hosts
body:
## Summary
AcquireAsync awaits the global semaphore first and then the host semaphore while still holding the global permit. With defaults 6 per host and 64 total, 100 downloads from one host leave 58 waiters holding global permits, so a request to an idle host waits although only 6 requests are on the wire. The global limit counts waiters instead of connections.

## Location
- `Runtime/RateLimit/ConcurrencyLimiter.cs:96`

## Problem
AcquireAsync awaits `_globalSemaphore.WaitAsync` (ConcurrencyLimiter.cs:96), marks globalAcquired, then awaits the host semaphore (:101) while still holding the global permit; it is released only if the host wait fails (:116-126). The comment says this order prevents starvation, and the XML docs define MaxTotalConnections as 'maximum total concurrent connections across all hosts' (:39-42) and the interceptor as limiting 'how many requests are on the wire' (Documentation~/Modules/Interceptors.md:194).

**Failure scenario.** Defaults 6 per host / 64 total. The app starts 100 downloads from cdn.example: 6 run, 58 more hold global permits while queued on the cdn host semaphore, 36 wait for a global permit. A request to api.example, which has nothing in flight, now waits behind them for a global permit until the CDN queue drains below 64, although only 6 requests are on the wire. The global limit counts waiters instead of connections.

## Suggested fix
Acquire the host permit first and the global permit second (a waiter then holds only a permit of its own host), or wait for both without holding either. Add a test: saturate host A with more waiters than the global limit and assert that host B is admitted.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The host permit is acquired first and the global permit second (or both are awaited without holding either), so a waiter holds only permits it can use
- [ ] A request to an idle host is admitted while another host is saturated with more waiters than the global limit
- [ ] Cancellation and failure paths release exactly the permits taken
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit test under Tests/Runtime/Performance/ saturates host A with more waiters than the global limit and asserts host B is admitted; it fails before the fix

title: [RateLimit] ConcurrencyLimiter.Release(string host) over-releases permits when called twice or without a matching acquire
body:
## Summary
ConcurrencyLimiter.Release looks up the host entry by string, releases its semaphore, decrements RefCount and always releases the global semaphore. A release for a host that was never acquired, or a second release for the same acquire, corrupts the global permit count and drives RefCount negative, so entries are never evicted or are evicted while a permit is held. Applications using the public limiter directly are affected.

## Location
- `Runtime/RateLimit/ConcurrencyLimiter.cs:150`

## Problem
Release looks the entry up by host string (ConcurrencyLimiter.cs:157-162), releases that semaphore and decrements RefCount (164-174, 257-266), then always releases the global semaphore and calls EndOperation (180-192). A host that was never acquired skips the host part but still releases a global permit (SemaphoreFullException, or one extra global permit) and decrements _activeOperations; a second Release for the same acquire over-releases the host semaphore and drives RefCount to -1, after which the entry is either never evicted or evicted while a permit is held (EvictIdleHostEntries_NoLock tests RefCount == 0, 275-298). The class doc (12-16) promises a release always returns to the semaphore it was taken from.

**Failure scenario.** Application code using the public limiter directly releases in a finally block after a failed AcquireAsync (cancelled wait): the global limit is raised by one for the limiter's lifetime and _activeOperations goes out of step, so a later Dispose can finalize while a real operation is still active.

## Suggested fix
Return a lease from AcquireAsync (IDisposable holding the HostEntry, idempotent Dispose) and make Release(string) internal or obsolete; this also removes the dictionary lookup under lock on release.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] AcquireAsync returns a lease (IDisposable) holding the host entry; Dispose is idempotent and releases the host and global permits exactly once
- [ ] Release(string) is made internal or marked obsolete, and a failed or cancelled AcquireAsync leaves no permit to release
- [ ] RefCount never goes below zero and the global limit never exceeds its configured value after double or unmatched release attempts
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/RateLimit/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [RateLimit] RequestQueue<T> and RequestPriority are public and unbounded but not used by any interceptor
body:
## Summary
RequestQueue<T> and RequestPriority are public API in TurboHTTP.RateLimit, yet no runtime code uses them (BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor has its own queue) and only a performance test references them. The queue has no capacity limit and its DequeueAsync and TryDequeue paths handle the consumed signal differently. Users may assume the pipeline supports request priorities, and the public surface must be kept compatible for no benefit.

## Location
- `Runtime/RateLimit/RequestQueue.cs:27`

## Problem
rg over Runtime, Samples~ and Documentation~ finds no use of RequestQueue<T> or RequestPriority outside RequestQueue.cs (BackgroundNetworkingInterceptor has its own BoundedRequestQueue); only Tests/Runtime/Performance/RequestQueueTests.cs references it. ConcurrencyInterceptor has no priority input. The queue has no capacity (ConcurrentQueue per priority, RequestQueue.cs:29, 67-77). DequeueAsync drops the consumed signal on its 'no item observed' path (110-112) while TryDequeue restores it (138-147).

**Failure scenario.** A user reading the RateLimit API assumes request priorities are supported by the pipeline and builds on RequestQueue<T>; nothing bounds it, and nothing in the client consumes it. It is 223 lines of public surface (about a third of the module) that must be kept compatible.

## Suggested fix
Make it internal or remove it until #118 wires priorities into an interceptor; if it stays public, give it a capacity and align the two dequeue paths.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] RequestQueue<T> and RequestPriority are made internal or removed until priorities are wired into an interceptor (#118), or, if kept public, the queue has a configurable capacity

title: [RateLimit] RequestQueue.Enqueue races Shutdown and can strand an accepted item behind a cancelled shutdown token
body:
## Summary
RequestQueue.Enqueue checks the shutdown flag, enqueues, increments the count and releases the semaphore with no exclusion against Shutdown. If Shutdown cancels the token between the check and the enqueue, the item is accepted without an exception but every later DequeueAsync throws OperationCanceledException, contrary to the documented drain-then-cancel behaviour.

## Location
- `Runtime/RateLimit/RequestQueue.cs:71`

## Problem
Enqueue checks _shutdown, then enqueues, increments _count and releases the semaphore with no exclusion against Shutdown (:69-76). Shutdown cancels _shutdownCts when _count is 0 (:157-161, :202-209). DequeueAsync links every wait to _shutdownCts.Token (:95-97), and SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync with an already cancelled token fails before it looks at the count. The same happens when the last counted item is dequeued between another Enqueue's ConcurrentQueue.Enqueue and its Interlocked.Increment. The only test covers TryDequeue signal restore (Tests/Runtime/Performance/RequestQueueTests.cs:12).

**Failure scenario.** Thread E passes the shutdown check; thread S calls Shutdown() on the empty queue and cancels the token; E completes its enqueue without an exception. Every later DequeueAsync throws OperationCanceledException although Count is 1: the accepted item is never delivered (only TryDequeue can still reach it), contrary to the documented drain-then-cancel behaviour.

## Suggested fix
Make the shutdown check and the enqueue atomic (a lock, or re-check _shutdown after the increment and undo/throw), and let DequeueAsync take available items before honouring the shutdown token.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The shutdown check and the enqueue are atomic, or Enqueue re-checks after the increment and throws/undoes, so no item is accepted and then stranded
- [ ] DequeueAsync returns available items before honouring the shutdown token
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/RateLimit/ fails before the fix and passes after it and covers the Enqueue/Shutdown interleaving without sleeps

title: [Retry] Retry condition (5xx, NetworkError, Timeout) is hard-coded in three places and RetryPolicy has no hook to change it
body:
## Summary
The 5xx range check is duplicated in RetryDetectorHandler, RetryTerminalObserverHandler and UHttpError.IsRetryable, and RetryPolicy exposes only counts and delays. RetryInterceptor copies the policy into a base RetryPolicy, so a subclass cannot change behaviour either. Callers cannot choose which statuses are retried without replacing the interceptor.

## Location
- `Runtime/Retry/RetryDetectorHandler.cs:70`

## Problem
'statusCode >= 500 && statusCode < 600' appears in RetryDetectorHandler.OnResponseStartAsync (RetryDetectorHandler.cs:70), RetryTerminalObserverHandler (RetryInterceptor.cs:189) and UHttpError.IsRetryable (Core/UHttpError.cs:76-82). RetryPolicy (RetryPolicy.cs:10-132) exposes counts and delays only: no status set, predicate or total time budget. RetryPolicy is unsealed but the interceptor copies it through an internal copy constructor into a base RetryPolicy (RetryInterceptor.cs:27), so a subclass cannot change behaviour. #118 covers 429 handling only.

**Failure scenario.** A 501 Not Implemented, 505, or a captive portal's 511 is retried three times with 1-2-4 s backoff (3.5-7 s with jitter) before the caller sees it; a 408 or 429 with Retry-After is never retried, and neither can be changed without replacing the interceptor (which third parties cannot write equivalently, #76).

## Spec reference
RFC 9110 section 15.6

## Suggested fix
Put the classification in one place (a RetryPolicy member such as RetryableStatusCodes or a ShouldRetry predicate with the current behaviour as default), use it from both handlers, and seal RetryPolicy.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The retry classification lives in one place (for example RetryPolicy.RetryableStatusCodes or a ShouldRetry predicate) with the current behaviour as default
- [ ] RetryDetectorHandler, RetryTerminalObserverHandler and UHttpError.IsRetryable use that single definition
- [ ] RetryPolicy is sealed or its extension point is honoured by the interceptor copy
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Retry/ fails before the fix and passes after it (or Tests/Runtime/Core/ for the classifier)

title: [Retry] RetryInterceptor retries every 5xx status including 501, 505 and 511 that cannot succeed on retry
body:
## Summary
RetryDetectorHandler suppresses and retries any status from 500 to 599. 501 Not Implemented, 505 HTTP Version Not Supported and 511 Network Authentication Required will not change on retry, so callers wait through all retries and backoff and the origin receives extra requests.

**Failure scenario.** GET to an endpoint that answers 501: the caller waits for three more attempts and about 3.5-7 s of backoff before receiving the same 501, and the origin receives four requests.

## Spec reference
RFC 9110 15.6

## Suggested fix
Limit status-based retries to 500, 502, 503 and 504 by default and make the set configurable on RetryPolicy.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] By default only 500, 502, 503 and 504 trigger status-based retries; 501, 505 and 511 are returned to the caller immediately

title: [Retry] Suppressed 5xx bodies are drained with a time-only budget and TransportBehaviorFlags.SelfDrainsResponseBody is never read
body:
## Summary
RetryDetectorHandler discards suppressed 5xx bodies through ResponseBodyDiscardHelper with a 2 second timeout and no byte limit, and Http11ResponseBodySource.DrainAsync reads to EOF unbounded. The SelfDrainsResponseBody flag that every transport sets is read nowhere, although architecture.md says the retry handler depends on it. A large 503 body can be downloaded on every attempt.

## Location
- `Runtime/Retry/RetryDetectorHandler.cs:117`

## Problem
Suppressed 5xx bodies go to ResponseBodyDiscardHelper.DiscardAsync with only a 2 s timeout (:115-120, RetryInterceptor.cs:17), which calls body.DrainAsync (Runtime/Core/Internal/ResponseBodyDiscardHelper.cs:31). Http11ResponseBodySource.DrainAsync reads to EOF with no byte limit (Runtime/Transport/Http1/Http11ResponseBodySource.cs:229-252); its byte-bounded drain exists only in DisposeAsync (:279-312). TransportBehaviorFlags.SelfDrainsResponseBody is set per request by every transport (Runtime/Transport/RawSocketTransport.cs:154, Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.cs:302) and read nowhere in Runtime, while architecture.md says RetryDetectorHandler depends on it.

**Failure scenario.** An origin or CDN answers 503 with a large body on a fast link: each suppressed attempt downloads up to 2 s worth of data (tens of MB on Wi-Fi) before the backoff starts, times MaxRetries, only to keep one connection reusable.

## Suggested fix
Dispose directly (the transport's bounded self-drain) when the flag is set or Length is large or unknown, or give DiscardAsync a byte budget. If the flag stays unused, delete it together with the per-request SetState in the transports and correct the architecture note.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The discard of a suppressed response body is byte-bounded, or uses the transport's bounded self-drain when SelfDrainsResponseBody is set or the length is large or unknown
- [ ] If the flag stays unused it is removed together with the per-request SetState in the transports, and architecture.md is corrected

title: [Retry] Retry-After delta-seconds above int.MaxValue is parsed as absent so the request is retried after normal backoff
body:
## Summary
ParseRetryAfter uses int.TryParse, so values such as 4294967296 fail to parse and the method returns null. The 5xx is then retried after the normal backoff instead of being returned to the caller as a delay above MaxDelay would be.

## Location
- `Runtime/Retry/RetryDetectorHandler.cs:134`

## Problem
ParseRetryAfter uses `int.TryParse(value, NumberStyles.None, ...)` (RetryDetectorHandler.cs:134-138); for a value such as 4294967296 this fails, the DateTimeOffset.TryParse fallback (:140-148) fails too, and the method returns null (:151). OnResponseStartAsync then marks the 5xx retryable with no Retry-After (:85-90) and RetryInterceptor waits only ComputeDelay's backoff (RetryInterceptor.cs:105-113). The cap logic that returns the response to the caller (:73-83) is bypassed. RetryAfterCapTests only use 86400 and 0.

**Failure scenario.** A 503 with `Retry-After: 4294967296` (or any 10+ digit value) is retried after about one second, three times, instead of being handed to the caller like `Retry-After: 86400` is.

## Spec reference
RFC 9110 10.2.3

## Suggested fix
Parse with long (digits only) and saturate; any value that overflows is 'greater than MaxDelay'. Add a test.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Retry-After digits are parsed as long with saturation; any overflowing value is treated as greater than MaxDelay and the response is returned to the caller
- [ ] Values at and around int.MaxValue and long.MaxValue are covered

title: [Retry] HTTP-date Retry-After is evaluated against the device clock instead of the response Date header
body:
## Summary
ParseRetryAfter computes the delay as the HTTP-date minus DateTimeOffset.UtcNow and ignores the response Date header. With a skewed device clock the delay is far too long (response returned without retry) or zero (retried too early).

## Location
- `Runtime/Retry/RetryDetectorHandler.cs:146`

## Problem
ParseRetryAfter computes `retryAt - DateTimeOffset.UtcNow` (RetryDetectorHandler.cs:140-148) and never reads the response's Date header, which the handler has in `headers`.

**Failure scenario.** The device clock is 10 minutes behind. A 503 with `Retry-After: <server now + 5 s>` yields a delay of 10 min 5 s, above the default 30 s MaxDelay, so the response is returned without any retry. With the clock ahead the delay is 0 and the request is retried earlier than the server asked. Confirm with a transport stub that sets Date and Retry-After and a skewed clock.

## Spec reference
RFC 9110 10.2.3

## Suggested fix
When the response has a valid Date, use Retry-After minus Date as the delay; fall back to the local clock only without it. Inject the clock so it is testable.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] When the response has a valid Date header the delay is Retry-After minus Date; the local clock is used only when Date is absent or invalid
- [ ] The clock is injectable so the behaviour is testable
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Retry/ fails before the fix and passes after it with a skewed clock and a stub transport setting Date and Retry-After

title: [Retry] RetryInterceptor allocates handlers, boxed state and an event dictionary for every request before the first attempt
body:
## Summary
For every retry-eligible request RetryInterceptor allocates a RetryDetectorHandler and a RetryTerminalObserverHandler up front, boxes the attempt number into context state and builds a Dictionary for the RetryAttempt event. This costs about five allocations (roughly 300 bytes) even when the first attempt succeeds.

## Location

## Problem
For every retry-eligible request the wrapper allocates a RetryDetectorHandler and a RetryTerminalObserverHandler up front (:45-50; the observer is used only on the last attempt), boxes the attempt number into context state (:55) and allocates a Dictionary with a boxed int for the RetryAttempt event (:56, :135-141).

**Failure scenario.** Every idempotent request through a client with RetryInterceptor pays about five allocations (roughly 300 bytes) although it succeeds on the first attempt.

## Suggested fix
Create the terminal observer lazily, record the first attempt without a data dictionary (or record attempts from the second on), and skip SetState for attempt 1.

## Acceptance criteria
